Namibia has officially recognised its first three Other Effective Area‑based Conservation Measures (OECMs), showing that conservation goes beyond protected areas. OECMs are places managed to deliver long‑term biodiversity conservation, even though they are not formally declared protected areas, proving that people and nature can thrive together across working landscapes.  ✅ NamibRand Nature Reserve ✅ ProNamib Nature Reserve ✅ Canyon Nature Park  Together, these sites conserve around 318,480 hectares of land managed for biodiversity.  The certification followed a national validation workshop in Windhoek led by @ministry_of_environment_nam with partners including @namibia_nature_foundation , @mfmrnamibia, WWF Namibia, communal conservancies and others, supporting Namibia’s progress toward the 30 by 30 biodiversity target.  @namib_rand @pro.namib   #WWFNamibia #OECMs #InclusiveConservation #30by30

The Youth Climate Change Conference 2025 was successfully held from 4–5 November 2025 at the Emirates Hotel in Ondangwa, Oshana Region. The conference was convened under the theme: “Our Climate, Our Responsibility: Namibian Youth on Climate Action.” It brought together a wide and diverse representation, including government ministries, local authorities, academia, development partners, traditional leaders, media, youth leaders, learners, and children, totalling an estimated 157 participants. The event was spearheaded by SOS Children’s Villages Namibia through the Eco-Champions Project, with collaboration from partners and youth-led environmental organisations such as Youth4CAN, NAYORE, Tulonga Foundation, and Wakapinya Environmental Education.  The main objectives of the convening were to: Increase awareness among young people on climate change, its impacts, and their role in mitigation and adaptation, Build capacity through knowledge transfer on climate-smart practices, green entrepreneurship, climate finance, and resilience-building, Strengthen collaboration between youth and key stakeholders, including the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism, development agencies, academia, and local authorities, Provide a platform for youth-led dialogue, innovation, skills development, and policy advocacy and, Develop actionable commitments from youth and stakeholders towards climate resilience and sustainable development in Namibia. All these were achieved through presentations on various issues affecting youth and the environment, panel discussions, exhibitions to inspire youth to become innovators of ideas and break-out sessions tailored to create dialogues amongst youth on climate change mitigation.   Read more: https://youthforcan.org.na/2025/11/21/youth-climate-change-conference-namibia-2025/

World Pangolin Day | 21 February   Today, Namibia joins the world in celebrating one of nature’s most unique and most threatened species: the pangolin. These shy, scale-covered mammals play a vital role in controlling insect populations and maintaining healthy ecosystems. Protecting them means protecting our biodiversity and supporting the community-led conservation efforts that make our country a global leader in conservation. LEGAL HUB: Minister Indileni Daniel on Friday launched the Sustainable Wildlife Management Programme Legal Hub in Windhoek, describing it as a strategic step forward in strengthening Namibia’s policy and legal framework for sustainable management of natural resources.   The hub is a website containing a collection of policy and legal documents relating to the governance and regulation of natural resources in Namibia. Namibia joins other countries with similar hubs, such as Botswana, Zambia and Zimbabwe, to mention a few.   The online hub is a central repository of information pertaining wildlife management laws that can be a dependable resource for scholars, practitioners, journalists and broader public. It was done in collaboration with FAO Namibia.

Diceros bicornis. The black rhino’s name tells its story. Diceros comes from the Greek di and ceros, meaning two horns, while bicornis comes from the Latin bi and cornis, also meaning two horns. A name rooted in form, strength and ancient lineage.  In Namibia’s Kunene Region, these remarkable animals have adapted to one of the harshest environments on earth. Desert-adapted black rhinos endure extreme temperatures, survive days without water, and feed on hardy plants that few other mammals can tolerate. They move quietly through open spaces shaped by rock, wind and time.  Photo credit: @Marcus Westberg  #SaveTheRhinoTrust #BlackRhino

At Gobabeb, we are committed to developing the skills of young emerging environmental scientists. Vianda Kauzuu, an intern from @nustnamibia , presenting her research proposal on evaluating the effects of solar-distilled grey water on vegetables grown in distinct soil conditions. Her project aligns with Namibia’s Sixth National Development Plan (NDP6), particularly Pillar 3: Environmental Sustainability. In a country as water scarce as Namibia, her research explores innovative solutions by reusing grey water, reducing freshwater demand and using solar distillation, which supports climate-smart agriculture and renewable energy use. If you happen to visit Gobabeb and are interested in her work, feel free to chat with her, she’s always happy to share insights about her project and its importance for farmers facing water scarcity.

Here at Gobabeb, we value partnership and collaboration. Dr. Stephan Getzin, one of Gobabeb’s research associates, and his team mapped ring formation in the grass species Eragrostis nindensis across numerous study sites in Namibia from 2023-2025, representing the first in-depth investigation of plant ring patterns in the country. Gobabeb continues to provide a platform for both Namibian and international researchers to engage, innovate and contribute to long-term environmental research in the Namib Desert. Link to publication: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140196326000601

BIOTRADE: Executive Director Sikongo Haihambo today revealed that Namibia’s biotrade sector contributes 4.5% to the national economy, with the country’s Devil’s Claw supplying 90% of the global market. Haihambo made the remarks at the opening of the Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) Sector Training currently under way in Windhoek. He emphasised the critical role of researchers in implementing the ABS framework, describing them as the first point of contact with Namibia’s biological and genetic resources. He also acknowledged regulators as the guardians of the country’s genetic resources. Additionally, he highlighted the essential role of the media in raising awareness about biopiracy, benefit sharing and community rights relating to genetic and biological resources. The training, which begins today, aims to equip researchers, regulators and media practitioners with knowledge on ABS, and will conclude on 16 April 2026.

REVENUE: The Ministry generated N$183 million in entrance and conservation fees from national parks during the 2025-2026 financial year. A further N$109 million was raised from conservancies through joint ventures, concessions and conservation hunting.  Meanwhile, N$4.4 million has been invested in infrastructure development. Staff housing and office facilities at Hardap Game Park, Namutoni, Keetmanshoop and Daan Viljoen Game Park have been renovated. In addition, 183km of fencing in Etosha National Park has been upgraded, while a further 15km and 13km of fencing have been completed in Mahango National Park.  The upgrades are intended to strengthen tourism infrastructure, support conservation and wildlife management, reduce human-wildlife conflict, and promote biodiversity.

COMMEMORATION: Minister Indileni Daniel joined stakeholders on Wednesday to commemorate the 2026 Environmental Knowledge Day under the theme “Driving Sustainable Impact Through Strategic Partnerships”. The event highlighted the importance of collaboration across government, the private sector and civil society in addressing Namibia’s environmental challenges, with a strong emphasis on partnerships as a driver of sustainable impact.  In line with this, First National Bank Namibia, through the FirstRand Namibia Group, committed N$4 million to the Community Conservation Fund of Namibia to support sustainable financing for conservation and rural development.  Minister Daniel reaffirmed the Ministry’s dedication to advancing Namibia’s environmental and climate resilience agenda, calling for strengthened partnerships, innovation and shared responsibility to secure a sustainable future for all. The event took place in Windhoek and was attended by Environmental Commissioner Timoteus Mufeti and other environmental and conservation stakeholders.

STRATEGIC: President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah said aviation is a strategic infrastructure that drives economic growth, facilitates trade and tourism, and connects African economies beyond it being just a mode of transport.   The President said this in a speech delivered on her behalf by Environment, Forestry and Tourism Minister Indileni Daniel on Wednesday morning during the 2026 Aviation Week Africa under way in Windhoek.   She further highlighted the urgent need to strengthen intra-African connectivity, reduce operational costs and move towards coordinated, continent wide solutions through initiatives such as the Single African Air Transport Market.  The event convenes aviation leaders and stakeholders under the theme “Linking Africa” and runs from Wednesday, 22 to 25 April 2026. Namibia wishes to advance its commitment to position itself as a regional gateway and logistics hub.

In September, SRT and Ecowings Namibia covered nearly 1,500 km and 6 flight hours to provide crucial aerial support for ground teams working in the Nyae Nyae Conservancy.   Our mission was to assist the @ministry_of_environment_nam Ministry of Environment and Tourism Namibia  and the Nyae Nyae Conservancy in checking for fence breaks and other challenges within this vast, rugged and remote area (roughly half the size of Wales). Our donkey team has been working tirelessly to seek out missing rhinos🤝  In September the team was sent on a mission to find a cow and calf in a remote ephemeral riverbed.  Within a few days news came back to base camp that they had succeeded – cow and calf are safe.  The two had moved off further down the river after good rains earlier this year have ensured plentiful food and water.   Several of the larger seasonal rivers in our north-west landscape still have pools of water, close to 9 months after the rains.  Abundant water makes our trackers’ jobs more difficult as rhinos move towards more remote areas.   Thank goodness our Donkey team can reach even the most well hidden rhinos – well done colleagues🥳🥳🥳

Over three days, key conservation stakeholders, including @ministry_of_environment_nam , conservancies, community forests, NGOs, researchers, and development partners, gathered in Windhoek to reflect on the past, assess the present, and shape the future of Namibia’s Community-Based Natural Resource Management #CBNRM programme.  The workshop unpacked several critical themes, including: 🔹 Governance and accountability within conservancies and community forests 🔹 Strengthening benefit-sharing and improving financial management systems 🔹 Enhancing tourism, concession, and joint-venture frameworks 🔹 Addressing human–wildlife conflict through community-led solutions 🔹 Modernising CBNRM data systems such as CONINFO, SMART, and digital monitoring tools 🔹 OECMs, landscape-level management, and transboundary conservation 🔹 Mining and land-use challenges in community conservation areas 🔹 Capacity building and accreditation through the NACSO Training Institute  These discussions were essential in charting a stronger, more accountable, and more resilient future for community conservation, ensuring that Namibia’s world-renowned CBNRM programme continues to deliver meaningful social, ecological, and economic benefits.

Earlier this month, our team set out to find a rhino that had not been seen for some time. With the help of a Piper Super Cub – an aircraft perfectly suited for low, slow and careful flying we took to the sky. Thanks to excellent air-to-ground communication using radios funded by the @namibia_nature_foundation Namibia Nature Foundation (NNF) , we located the animal just 30 minutes after take-off. Our ground team Jason and Epson once again proved why boots on the ground and skilled foot-tracking techniques remain irreplaceable in the work we do.   Now that we know this rhino is alive and well, we are focusing our patrol efforts on poaching hot-spot areas, especially after the heartbreaking loss of a cow and calf to poachers in October.  An eye in the sky played a key role in this successful search. Random aerial patrols not only help us locate rhinos faster, but also act as a deterrent to poachers and improve our reaction time. A huge thank you to Save the Rhino International for providing the funding to build this new capacity within SRT, and to all the supporters and funders who are contributing to our new air wing.   Special thanks to David Francis and his Super Cub for professional airmanship and some unforgettable views!  #savetherhinotrust #conservation #savetherhinointernational #namibianaturefoundation

Weekly Teacher Spotlight!  My name is Helena Frans. I was born and raised in Iishanaputa Uukolonkadhi, a small village in the Omusati region. I started my schooling at Iishanaputa Combined School from Grade 1 to 10, and completed my secondary education (Grade 11–12) at Mwaala High School.  Due to financial challenges, my parents could no longer afford for me to continue my studies. I stayed at home and began searching for work. In 2021, my uncle called me from the north to come stay with his daughter at Naankuse Lodge.   In 2023, a daycare was opened on the farm for all the babies, and I continued working as a house helper for my uncle. I didn’t give up.   A few months later, a vacancy for a school cleaner opened at Naankuse Primary School. I submitted my CV, and within a week, I was told I could start the following Monday. That’s where my journey truly began in 2023.   I didn’t stop at cleaning, I also helped in the daycare, assisted teachers with marking learners’ test papers, and supported learners with their homework. In October 2024, during a meeting with our boss, Mrs. Marlice van Vuuren, we were asked where we see ourselves in five years.  I shared my dream of becoming a teacher. My colleagues supported me because they had seen my passion and dedication, especially how I worked with learners and assisted in the Grade 1 class. As of June 2025, I was appointed as a Grade 0 & 1 Class Assistant.   In January 2026, I began my role as a pre-primary teacher. In February 2026, I joined Alison online learning and earned two certificates in Early Childhood Development.   I still dream of studying further and becoming a graduate. I believe my skills, dedication, and willingness to learn make me a strong future leader. I am proud of my journey and excited to keep growing with the Naankuse family.  Stories like Helena’s are made possible through support and opportunity. Small spotted genets 💛  Adorable, a little feisty, and ready for their next chapter in the wild.  At N/a’an ku sê, we often welcome these beautiful creatures after they’ve been orphaned or rescued from conflict situations. After spending time in rehabilitation at our Wildlife Sanctuary, they get a second chance at life where they truly belong — in the wild.  On Saturday, 11 April 2026, four of our furry friends took that big step. Carefully sedated, with two fitted with VHF tracking collars, and safely transported to Neuras Wine and Wildlife Estate — a perfect place to call home.  For now, they’ll settle into a soft-release camp, giving them time to adjust to their new surroundings. And soon… complete freedom. 🌿✨
